entry.title: pi-provider-opencode-console: live OpenCode Go models without waiting for pi releases
entry.summary: pi-provider-opencode-console adds OpenCode Console and OpenCode Go to pi with OAuth device-code login and a live model catalog, so you no longer wait for a pi release to refresh its static model list.
entry.content:
For my personal work I use the OpenCode Go subscription as the model provider in pi. And there was one detail that annoyed me every week: when OpenCode changed the subscription model catalog, pi kept showing me the old list until a new release shipped.

The problem: a model list frozen into the binary¶

pi does not discover models at runtime for its built-in providers. The catalog lives in pi-ai, in a file generated at build time:

// This file is auto-generated by scripts/generate-models.ts
// Do not edit manually - run 'npm run generate-models' to update

For a provider with a public API and a stable catalog that's fine. For a subscription that adds and retires models every few weeks, it's constant friction: you see new names on the OpenCode site that don't exist in /model, and retired models that are still there taking up space.

The alternative was hand-editing models.json, which is worse: you maintain it, it drifts, and model overrides don't always behave the same way with extension providers.

The fix: device-code OAuth and a live catalog¶

pi-provider-opencode-console is a pi extension that registers two new providers — opencode-console and opencode-go-console — with OAuth 2.0 device authorization grant login (RFC 8628) and model discovery against OpenCode's real catalog.

pi install npm:pi-provider-opencode-console

The two providers are deliberately distinct from the ones pi ships with:

Provider Auth Model catalog
opencode / opencode-go (built-in) API key Static, compiled into pi-ai
opencode-console / opencode-go-console (extension) OAuth device code Live, from the server

That leaves the built-in providers untouched and lets you pick whichever matches your setup: API key or subscription. No name collisions, no credential conflicts.

Login¶

The flow is the usual one: you request the login, pi gives you a code and a URL, you approve in the browser, done.

/login opencode-go-console

# pi prints a user code and the verification URL
# you approve in the browser and the credential lands in ~/.pi/agent/auth.json

For the full console (the one that absorbed Zen) it's the same flow:

/login opencode-console

Both share the device-code session, so authenticating one leaves the other ready. The credential is stored as oauth in auth.json, and the access token renews itself: with less than five minutes to expiry the extension refreshes before the next request, single-flight so two concurrent calls don't request two tokens, and mirrors the rotated token into the sibling entry.

One important thing: the extension is OAuth-only. It does not offer pi's generic "Enter API key" login. If you want API-key access with a static list, that's exactly why the built-in providers exist.

Where the models come from¶

Each provider has its own source:

  • opencode-go-console pulls the public GET https://opencode.ai/inference/go/v1/models catalog, the lite list, and enriches it with models.dev data while dropping disabled or deprecated ids.
  • opencode-console pulls the org-scoped GET {server}/api/config endpoint with Authorization: Bearer and x-org-id, so each organization sees the models it actually has.

To refresh without logging in again:

/opencode-go-console refresh

And to see what's behind it:

/opencode-go-console status    # auth method, account, org, token expiry
/opencode-go-console logout    # clears the Go credential, keeps Console's

The console provider also has switch-org to change organization when the session isn't already scoped to one from the browser. If the grant requested org scoping, switch-org doesn't apply: you log in again.

The detail that makes this work well¶

OpenCode does not expose every model over the same protocol. Some models speak anthropic-messages, others openai-completions, others openai-responses, and the Gemini ones go through google-generative-ai. The extension routes each request to the right wire API for the model you picked, and normalizes the base URL per API kind before letting the SDK compose its own:

API kind Normalized base
anthropic-messages /inference[/go]/anthropic
openai-completions /inference[/go]/openai/v1
openai-responses /inference[/go]/openai/v1
google-generative-ai /inference[/go]/google/v1beta

Streaming and parsing are delegated to pi-ai's implementations instead of being reimplemented. That means a new model speaking an already-supported protocol works without touching the extension, and streaming bugs get fixed where they belong: in pi-ai.

It also injects per-request identity headers (x-opencode-org-id, x-opencode-client, x-opencode-request), which is what makes the session recognizable as yours on OpenCode's side.

Configuration¶

Just two environment variables, and usually none:

Variable Default What for
OPENCODE_CONSOLE_SERVER https://opencode.ai/console Self-hosted consoles. Persisted to auth.json on first sign-in.
PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR ~/.pi/agent pi's agent directory. Useful for testing in an isolated setup.

Migrating from older versions¶

2.0 broke compatibility on purpose: service-key auth (sk-…) was removed. If you still have one of those entries in auth.json, it's inert and pi reports "Provider is not configured". Delete it and do the device-code sign-in.

# coming from 1.x? check and clean up
cat ~/.pi/agent/auth.json

How I use it¶

I run pi on two machines with two different budgets: the OpenCode Go subscription for personal work and the Claude subscription for work (that's pi-claude-bridge). On the personal machine, this extension removed an entire class of friction: there's no longer a "let's see if this week's release brings the new model" moment.

The catalog you see in /model is the one you're paying for right now. If OpenCode adds a model in the morning, I have it in pi after a refresh, without updating anything.

And if you want to know how each of those models performs before picking one, aa-opencode crosses the catalog with Artificial Analysis benchmarks.

Resources¶

  • pi-provider-opencode-console on GitHub — Code and docs
  • On npm — pi install npm:pi-provider-opencode-console
  • OpenCode Console — The console and model catalog
  • RFC 8628 — OAuth 2.0 Device Authorization Grant
  • What is pi? — First part of the pi series

entry.title: aa-opencode: OpenCode models with benchmarks and price in one table
entry.summary: aa-opencode crosses the OpenCode model catalog with Artificial Analysis benchmarks and prints one table with intelligence, speed, and price per model. A Python CLI I just published.
entry.content:
I use OpenCode as one of the model providers in pi, and there's the problem: the list of available models is long and says nothing. You get names, sure. What you don't get is how well each one reasons, how fast it answers, or what a million tokens costs you. Picking by eye is a coin toss.

Artificial Analysis publishes exactly that: independent intelligence, coding, and math indices, plus output speed, time to first token, and price. But it has its own catalog and its own names, so crossing it by hand against OpenCode's models is a chunk of work every time you want to check.

So I wrote aa-opencode: it grabs the OpenCode model list, crosses it with the Artificial Analysis API, and prints a table. Nothing else. It's about 430 lines of Python with httpx and rich.

Installation¶

uv tool install git+https://github.com/pcaro/aa-opencode

It needs an Artificial Analysis API key, which is free: create an account, generate the key, and put it in the environment.

export ARTIFICIAL_ANALYSIS_API_KEY="your-key"

It also reads AA_API_KEY, and if you want to pass it ad hoc there's --api-key.

Usage¶

# Default table, sorted by intelligence
aa-opencode

# Other sort keys
aa-opencode --sort price
aa-opencode --sort speed
aa-opencode --sort coding

# JSON to chain into something else
aa-opencode --format json

By default it pulls the Go catalog. For the Zen catalog:

aa-opencode --catalog zen

What comes out¶

The Go catalog has 33 models with data in Artificial Analysis. The first thing that jumps out is that the smartest model in the catalog isn't the one I'd use for coding every day. gemini-4-argon-contributor leads with a 52.6 index and costs $8.0 per million. mimo-v2.6-pro scores 46.3 and costs $0.5. Sixteen times less for 11% less index.

On coding it flips. mimo-v2.5 scores 60.2 on the coding index at $0.2 per million, and muse-spark-1.2-contributor scores 58.6 at $0.1. Those are models I would never have considered opening without seeing those numbers side by side.

Speed: claude-haiku-5-5 runs at 238.9 tok/s and deepseek-v4.1-flash at 216.1. But look at the first one's TTFT: 285.8 seconds. That's not time to first token, it's an artifact of the test (queues, rate limits, whatever happened that day). TTFT from the API has to be read with tongs.

And price. OpenCode's price doesn't come from Artificial Analysis: it comes from models.dev, which is the source OpenCode uses for its catalog. Comparing the two, there are models where OpenCode charges you noticeably less than the public reference: mimo-v2.5 68% less, longcat-2.0 60% less, deepseek-v4.1-flash 50% less.

Zen is a different picture. There the top models run $20 per million (claude-fable-5-1, gpt-6-astra), and the quality/price ranking fills up with models that don't even show in Go.

Four Go models have no Artificial Analysis data: omen-alpha, hy4-preview, longcat-2.5-preview-free, and beam-free. They're previews and free models, so that's expected. In JSON they show up with matched: false, and in the human table you list them with --show-unmatched.

How it matches models¶

OpenCode IDs and Artificial Analysis slugs almost never match, so the matcher tries three things in order:

Exact slug. gpt-5.4 against gpt-5.4. Normalizing first: lowercase, dots to dashes, and everything non-alphanumeric stripped.

Substring. If one contains the other, it keeps the shortest slug, which is the most specific one. That's where things like gemini-4-argon-contributor → gemini-4-argon land.

Token set. For reordered names, like haiku-4-5 against 4-5-haiku.

It's pure heuristics, there's no hand-written equivalence table. It works well enough, but a badly matched model gives you believable, wrong numbers, which is the worst kind of error. When OpenCode adds new models, it's worth eyeballing the row before trusting it.

What it doesn't do¶

  • It doesn't tell you which model suits you. It just puts the numbers together and sorts them.
  • It doesn't check availability: if a model is down, it won't notice.
  • It keeps no history. Every run is a snapshot.
  • There's no manual equivalence table, so odd matches are possible.

Using the free Artificial Analysis API requires attribution, so: benchmarks come from Artificial Analysis and OpenCode pricing from models.dev.

Original source: github.com/pcaro/aa-opencode

entry.title: HarnessTax: The Harness Matters Less Than You Think
entry.summary: The HarnessTax study from UC Berkeley and Arena evaluates 21 model-harness pairings and reaches three surprising conclusions. They back up with data why I use pi and OpenCode daily.
entry.content:
When you pick a coding agent, you're not just choosing a model: you're also choosing its harness, the software that manages tools, context, and task execution. What if switching harnesses improves results or cuts the bill? That's the question HarnessTax asks. The study from UC Berkeley and Arena evaluates 21 model–harness pairs (Claude Code, Codex CLI, and pi, across 7 models) on SWE-bench Lite and Terminal-Bench 2.0: 30 random tasks per benchmark, 3 attempts per task.

Its three main conclusions are quite surprising:

1. The harness barely affects success rate, but it does affect cost¶

The same model achieves nearly identical success rates across different harnesses, but cost can vary up to 5x. The clearest case: Claude Fable 5 solves 97.8% of attempts in Claude Code and 96.7% in pi... but Claude Code costs twice as much ($1.33 vs $0.67). On average, Claude Code comes out 2x more expensive than pi on SWE-bench Lite and 1.5x on Terminal-Bench 2.0. They call that price difference for practically the same quality a harness tax.

2. A simple harness can be competitive¶

Pi reaches the Pareto frontier on both benchmarks with just four tools: read, write, edit, and bash. The key is at startup: Claude Code's mean initial context is over 10x pi's, with longer instructions and fatter tool schemas. That overhead is paid on every model call. Less scaffolding, same result.

3. Models can perform better outside their provider's harness¶

This is the most groundbreaking one. Even though OpenAI says GPT-5-Codex is optimized for Codex, in 9 of the 12 comparisons between Anthropic and OpenAI models, the best success rate is achieved with a harness other than the provider's own. For example, GPT-5.6 Sol gets an 83.3% success rate in pi versus 78.9% in Codex... at half the price. A model's capabilities are portable; the provider-harness coupling guarantees nothing.

What this means for me¶

For anyone using coding agents daily, the takeaway is clear: compare harnesses before accepting the default one, or you'll be paying the harness tax without noticing.

And for me personally, the study is a data-backed validation of what I already suspected. I've been using pi as my main agent for months —I explained what it is and why it convinced me— and OpenCode as a complement. The study confirms exactly why: a minimalist harness, with just the right tools and minimal initial context, delivers the same result as the heavyweight all-in-one agents at a fraction of the cost. The pi trilogy on this blog ages better than I expected.

Original source: HarnessTax: How Much Does the Harness Matter for Coding Agents? (UC Berkeley / Arena, September 2026). There's also an extended version on Arena's blog.

entry.title: What is Pi? — The Minimal Coding Agent That Went Viral
entry.summary: Pi is a minimal terminal coding agent. This article explains what it is, how it differs from Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, and Gemini CLI, and why it went viral.
entry.content:
I've been using pi as my primary coding agent for several months now. It's one of those tools that, once you use it, you can't imagine how you worked before. In this article —the first of a three-part series— I'll explain what pi is, how it differs from other coding agents, and why it has become extremely popular on GitHub. Don't miss pi.dev — the site has great animations that explain the concepts visually.

The philosophy: less is more¶

Pi defines itself as "a minimal terminal coding harness". And when they say minimal, they mean it.

The core of pi has exactly five native capabilities: read files, run Bash, edit files, write files, and manage sessions. That's it. No subagents, no plan mode, no permission popups, no built-in MCP, no code editor.

It sounds like little, but that's the whole point. We live in the age of harness engineering — the discipline of building robust environments around AI agents — and pi is an excellent starting point for building your own harness without paying the toll of a closed ecosystem.

Pi's philosophy is that you should adapt the tool to your workflows, not the other way around. Instead of shipping with 50 features most people don't use, pi gives you the minimal primitives and a TypeScript extension system to build exactly what you need.

Want subagents? Install an extension. Want MCP? Set up an adapter. Want plan mode? Write a prompt template. And if you don't want any of that, it doesn't take up space or slow down startup.

Comparison with other coding agents¶

Feature Pi Claude Code Codex OpenCode Gemini CLI
Philosophy Minimal core + extensions Everything included Everything included Minimal core Everything included
Models Any provider (API key or subscription) Claude only OpenAI only Multiple (OpenAI API) Gemini only
Subagents Via extensions Built-in Built-in Built-in Built-in
MCP Via extensions Built-in - Built-in Built-in
Plan mode Via skills/templates Built-in Built-in - -
Extensions TypeScript SDK JSON plugins - - -
Price Free (your keys) Paid subscription Paid subscription Free (your keys) Free (generous free tier)
Platform Terminal (any emulator) Terminal Terminal Terminal Terminal
Tree sessions Native (JSONL tree) Linear Linear Linear Linear
Skills Markdown + frontmatter Markdown + frontmatter - - -

Claude Code — Anthropic's all-in-one¶

Claude Code is Anthropic's official coding agent. It comes with everything: subagents, persistent memory, permission system, native MCP, and a very polished experience. It's the most mature non-IDE agent.

The catch: it only works with Claude. If you want to use DeepSeek, Gemini, or OpenAI, you can't. And the plugin ecosystem is limited compared to pi.

Codex — ChatGPT integration¶

Codex is OpenAI's agent. You can use it from the terminal (codex) or integrated with ChatGPT. It comes with subagents and a similar experience to Claude Code.

But same as Claude Code, you're locked to one provider. And extensions are practically nonexistent: what you see is what you get.

Gemini CLI — The community CLI¶

Gemini CLI comes from the google-gemini community project and integrates with Google's ecosystem (Gemini API, Google Cloud). Google has been gradually moving away from the CLI in favor of Antigravity, its proprietary enterprise client. It comes with skills and subagents, but customization is limited and third-party extensions are practically nonexistent.

OpenCode — The kindred spirit¶

OpenCode is the one I use most after pi, and in many ways it's its natural complement. Its philosophy is similar: minimal core, terminal-native, multi-model. It doesn't have pi's extension ecosystem, but it comes with built-in subagents and MCP. Written in Go, starts just as fast, and its OpenAI ecosystem integration is excellent.

What makes pi unique¶

After trying them all, what makes pi unique is a combination of factors that no other agent brings together:

Extensibility: With the TypeScript SDK you can add tools, commands, intercept events, create custom UI, and share it all as pi packages. No one else offers this level of customization.

Tree sessions: Conversations are saved as a decision tree. Use /tree to jump to any previous point and create an alternative branch without losing progress. Only pi has this.

Skills and prompt templates: Small markdown files that inject into the agent's context. The simplest way to teach your agent new capabilities. I already covered how to install them and Matt Pocock's viral skills.

Package ecosystem: pi.dev/packages has extensions for almost everything: MCP adapters, web search, context optimization modes, themes, and more. And if you can't find what you need, you write a TypeScript extension in five minutes.

It's not an IDE: Pi is an agent that lives in your terminal, not an editor. This means it works the same on your local machine, on a server over SSH, inside tmux, or on WSL. You use your favorite editor and pi handles the rest. I'll dive deeper into this concept in the next part of the series.

Why I like pi¶

By now it's probably obvious, but to wrap up: I like pi because I live in the terminal. Because I want to try many models without being locked to one provider. Because I customize everything with my own extensions.

It's not for everyone, obviously. If you prefer to pay a subscription and forget about it, Claude Code or Codex are more straightforward. But if you're an engineer who lives in the terminal, pi is probably the best coding agent out there today.

In the next articles of this series: - Pi from Beginner to Advanced — Installation, TUI, sessions, skills, extensions, and everything you need to master it. - The Pi Extensions I Use — My real setup with packages, skills, and custom extensions.

Source: pi.dev

entry.title: Crit: The Review Loop for Agents
entry.summary: Crit is a tool designed to close the code review loop for AI-generated code, providing an intuitive and efficient web interface.
entry.content:
Reviewing what an AI agent writes directly in the terminal is often a nightmare. You can't point to a specific line, provide structured feedback, and when the agent updates the file, you have to re-read everything to see what actually changed.

That's where Crit comes in.

Crit opens files generated or modified by your agent in the browser with a GitHub-style interface. You can leave comments on specific lines, suggestions for changes, and, best of all, see diffs between different iteration rounds.

What I liked most is its multi-agent nature and its usability. It doesn't matter if you use Claude Code, Cursor, Aider, or, as in my case, OpenCode. Crit integrates beautifully.

Installation and Setup¶

Installation is as simple as:

gah install tomasz-tomczyk/crit

Once installed, integrating it with OpenCode is just a matter of one command:

crit install opencode

This installs the necessary commands and skills for agents to use Crit. By running /crit in OpenCode, the review loop begins: the agent proposes a plan or changes, Crit opens the web interface for you to approve or correct, and the agent receives your structured feedback in a .crit.json file to act accordingly.

Note to my future self: If you use pi-agent instead of OpenCode, you can copy the OpenCode command as a prompt and copy the crit skill as-is — it works perfectly. In fact, this very annotation was reviewed using pi-agent with Crit.

Why Use It¶

  • Web Interface, not TUI: Markdown rendering and persistent visual diffs.
  • Round-to-round diffs: You see exactly what has changed since your last comment.
  • Agent agnostic: Works with any tool, allowing for a consistent workflow.
  • Direct suggestions: You can insert suggestions that the agent can apply as-is.

For example, the very change that fixed the comma issue in this annotation:

It is undoubtedly the missing piece to make working with agents truly collaborative rather than a succession of copy-pasting and tedious manual reviews.
